source: Amodio, Brea, Farrar, Ostojic, Clayton et al. (2021) Little evidence that Eurasian jays protect their caches by responding to cues about a conspecific's desire and visual perspective
finding: Five experiments in the original lab, mostly with the same birds, failed to reproduce the jay cache-protection effects (hide in out-of-view tray; avoid food the watcher is sated on) and found no integration of both cues.
numbers: 14 adult Eurasian jays from two colonies; 5 experiments. In 4 of 7 directional tests the result went the wrong way. In the other 3 (Exp 3, 4, 5 barrier) it was in the predicted direction but non-significant and much smaller than the original effects.
quote: raise questions about the reliability of the previously reported effects
limits: Low power with tiny samples; birds were about 5 years older than in the originals. Authors say no extremely large effect exists and original effects may be inflated by underpowered work plus publication bias.
agent_relevance: Warning for any animal ToM claim used as design evidence: small-N single-lab effects may not be real. Do not build scaffold operators on them.

source: Amodio et al. (2021) Discussion: methods lessons for comparative cognition
finding: Authors argue success of a replication cannot be judged by significance alone when replications are as small as the originals. They list reliability issues: low power, reuse of one aging bird sample, publication bias.
numbers: Exp 1-2 tested integration of two cues (visual perspective plus desire) with set-ups close to the originals. In Exp 1 the Different Food condition did not exceed chance for the out-of-view tray.
limits: One captive colony cannot be enlarged; no equivalence tests as the main frame.
agent_relevance: Treat 'positive in one lab' as low-confidence evidence; ask for multi-site replication before importing a mechanism.

source: Ostojic, Legg, Shaw, Cheke, Mendl, Clayton (2017) Current desires of conspecific observers affect cache-protection strategies in California scrub-jays and Eurasian jays
finding: Cachers preferentially cached the food the observer was not sated on, and did so even when they could not see which food the observer was sated on. So a response to the observer's overt behaviour at caching is a live rival to desire attribution.
numbers: Pilfering experiment n=16 (10 scrub-jays, 6 Eurasian jays), permutation test p<0.001. Caching experiment n=16 (9 scrub-jays, 7 Eurasian jays): p=0.006 (seen) and p=0.003 (unseen). Seen vs unseen did not differ (p=0.255).
limits: This is the original effect Amodio 2021 failed to replicate in Eurasian jays. Authors themselves note the behaviour-cue explanation.
agent_relevance: Same pattern as LLM ToM: cues in the input can mimic mental-state reasoning; test by removing the cue.

source: Clayton, Dally, Emery (2007) Social cognition by food-caching corvids. The western scrub-jay as a natural psychologist
finding: Review of the Emery and Clayton re-caching work: experienced thieves re-cache items an observer saw, naive birds do not. Jays also track which individual watched which caching event.
numbers: Barrier experiment: Friedman chi2(2)=2.57, n=8, p=0.03; out-of-view tray beat full-view tray (Dunnett q=2.9, p<0.05). Observer vs observer-control re-caching: sign test S=6/6, p=0.03 vs S=4/6, p=0.69. About 25% of items still went to the full-view tray.
limits: Samples of 6 to 8 birds; sign test on 6 animals. Authors admit a more elaborate behaviour-cueing account cannot be fully excluded.
agent_relevance: Experience projection (use own thief experience to model another) is an interesting design idea but rests on very small samples.

source: Penn and Povinelli (2007) On the lack of evidence that non-human animals possess anything remotely resembling a 'theory of mind'
finding: Argues that competitive-paradigm results (chimps, corvids) can be explained by perceptual-cue and learned-rule accounts. No protocol so far discriminates behaviour-reading from mental-state representation.
numbers: No new data; critical review. Says the set of perceptual cues (face or eye direction, body position) is sufficient to explain the subjects' behaviour.
quote: it is also possible for the same behaviour to be produced without an f ToM of any kind
limits: Position paper. Later work (Bugnyar 2016, Kano 2019) built tests that answer its critique.
agent_relevance: Gives the discriminating-test logic to copy for LLM evals: remove surface cues, then see if behaviour survives.

source: Bugnyar (2011) Knower-guesser differentiation in ravens: others' viewpoints matter
finding: Ravens predicted which bystander (seen at both, one, or no caching events) would pilfer. Performance dropped when the competitor's view was blocked independently of the subject's own view; behavioural-cue controls had no effect.
numbers: Informed vs uninformed competitor: Wilcoxon n=8 (2 ties), p=0.023. Partially informed: cache choice sign test 6/6 non-ties, p=0.032. Matching caches to competitors in informed condition 7/7, p=0.016; uninformed 4/7, p=1.
limits: Tiny n (7 to 10 birds). Some binomial tests only p=0.055 to 0.063. Stay treatment showed no preference (5 ties of 5).
agent_relevance: Blocking only the competitor's view is a good template for what-others-know tests.

source: Bugnyar, Reber, Buckner (2016) Ravens attribute visual access to unseen competitors
finding: Ravens guarded caches when they heard conspecifics and a peephole was open, not when it was closed, with no gaze cue to read. They generalised from own seeing experience.
numbers: n=9 ravens. Time to finish cache chi2(2)=14.889, p<0.001; peephole vs non-observed Z=-2.666, p=0.012 (Bonferroni); revisit-and-improve Z=2.539, p=0.024. Peephole vs observed not different (p=0.08; p=0.94). Placing caches outside the open peephole's view: 1.78 in view vs 2.78 out of view, p=0.297.
limits: Birds did not use barrier geometry, so understanding is limited. One lab, n=9, no independent replication found this session.
agent_relevance: Best corvid evidence against pure behaviour-reading, but only for 'could be seen', not for what others believe.

source: Kano, Krupenye, Hirata, Tomonaga, Call (2019) Great apes use self-experience to anticipate an agent's action in a false-belief test
finding: Goggles-style control inside an eye-tracked false-belief test. Only apes who had experienced the barrier as opaque anticipated the actor's mistaken search. The barrier looked identical from afar for both groups, so behaviour cues cannot explain it.
numbers: n=47 apes (opaque n=23; see-through n=24), between subjects. Opaque group: P=0.033 (r about 0.35 as extracted) and P=0.019 in follow-up tests; see-through group n.s. (P=0.42).
limits: Anticipatory looking has had replication trouble in infants; modest N; between subjects.
agent_relevance: Strongest answer so far to the behaviour-rule account: self-experience transfer with no extra cue.

source: Buttelmann, Buttelmann, Carpenter, Call, Tomasello (2017) Great apes distinguish true from false beliefs in an interactive helping task
finding: Apes helped an experimenter differently in false-belief and true-belief conditions. The false-belief result replicated in Study 2 against an ignorance control (apes chose at chance there).
numbers: Study 1: false-belief 76.5% vs true-belief 53.1% correct box; U=74.50, N=17 per group, p=.015, r=.42. Study 2: false-belief 72.0%, p=.006, r=.74; ignorance 49.9%, p=.877; difference U=55.00, p=.027, r=.41. No learning over trials (p=.467, .959).
limits: Between subjects, n=17 per cell, 6 trials each. Apes only, no corvids.
agent_relevance: Compare belief against an ignorance control, not just against no condition.

source: Karg, Schmelz, Call, Tomasello (2016) Differing views: Can chimpanzees do Level 2 perspective-taking?
finding: Chimps seemed to pass a mistaken-perspective stick game, but a follow-up showed they projected their own preference onto the competitor. Six-year-old children tracked the other's view.
numbers: Chimps picked the bigger stick (empty after the competitor chose) in M=60% of trials, above chance (t(15)=2.60, p=.02). Children M=28%. In a follow-up where chimps had no preference they chose randomly.
limits: Compares two species with different baselines. Own-preference rule fits chimp data.
agent_relevance: Own-preference projection is a cheap non-mentalising baseline; LLMs can do the same, so control for it.

source: Chimpanzees gesture to humans in mirrors: using reflection to dissociate seeing from line of gaze
finding: Chimps gestured more when an experimenter could see them via a mirror even without direct line of gaze, suggesting experience projection from their own mirror experience.
numbers: Exact statistics not extracted this session.
limits: Authors discuss low-level alternatives; single lab.
agent_relevance: Same discriminating logic (seeing without gaze) used in another species.

source: Hare, Call, Tomasello (2001) Do chimpanzees know what conspecifics know?
finding: Founding competitive-paradigm chimp study. Only front matter appeared in search results; full text not read.
numbers: not read this session
limits: A later Hare et al. 2006 critique (via search summary) says early results may reflect inflexible approach to food near barriers. Karg 2016 shows own-preference projection can explain related tasks.
agent_relevance: Background only.

source: Hare et al. (2002) Do capuchin monkeys know what conspecifics do and do not see?
finding: Adapted the chimp competitive method to capuchins. Search summary says authors frame it as a replication and species-comparison method. Outcome not read.
numbers: not read this session
limits: Snippet only.
agent_relevance: Background only.

source: Krachun et al. (2009) chimpanzee visual-perspective study, Animal Cognition
finding: Search summary: tested chimpanzees' understanding of visual angles; a secondary aim was replicating Call and Carpenter (2001). Details not read.
numbers: not read this session
limits: Snippet only.
agent_relevance: Background only.

source: Krupenye, Kano, Hirata, Call, Tomasello (2016) Great apes anticipate that other individuals will act according to false beliefs
finding: Eye-tracking study of apes watching actors with false beliefs. Later work (Kano 2019, Buttelmann 2017) builds on it. Full text not read this session.
numbers: not read this session
limits: Anticipatory looking is criticised as possibly driven by low-level cues; Kano 2019 was designed to answer this.
agent_relevance: Background only.

source: Kosinski (2024) Evaluating large language models in theory of mind tasks (PNAS)
finding: Newer LLMs solve false-belief tasks designed for humans, with a sharp jump across model generations.
numbers: 40 tasks (Unexpected Contents and Unexpected Transfer). GPT-3 davinci-003 and ChatGPT-3.5-turbo solved 20%; ChatGPT-4 solved 75%, matching 6-year-old children.
limits: Passing text vignettes is not proof of ToM; tasks may appear in training data; Ullman and Shapira show brittleness.
agent_relevance: Treat high ToM benchmark scores as weak evidence; use perturbation tests.

source: Ullman (2023) Large Language Models Fail on Trivial Alterations to Theory-of-Mind Tasks
finding: Small changes that keep the ToM logic (transparent container, protagonist who cannot read, uninformative label) flip GPT-3.5 answers. The author argues outlying failures should outweigh average success.
numbers: Example altered vignette: P(popcorn)=10% vs P(chocolate)=87%. A double-space prompt change moved the original vignette to chocolate 53% vs 39%.
limits: Single model family, few vignettes, no human baseline; reports probabilities, not accuracy.
agent_relevance: LLM version of Penn and Povinelli: passing standard tasks may hide failure on the discriminating variant.

source: Shapira et al. (2023) Clever Hans or Neural Theory of Mind? Stress testing social reasoning in LLMs
finding: Across 6 ToM tasks LLMs show some ability but it is not robust. They fail adversarial variants, suggesting shallow heuristics.
numbers: Some datasets near ceiling (TriangleCOPA 96% by flan-t5-xxl), others much lower. Exact per-task numbers not extracted.
limits: 2023 models; later models not all covered.
agent_relevance: The Clever Hans warning: use adversarial and cue-removed items before trusting a ToM-style operator.

source: Kim et al. (2023) FANTOM: A benchmark for stress-testing machine theory of mind in interactions
finding: In multi-party conversations with information asymmetry, models answer simple belief questions but fail matched questions needing the same reasoning (who had access to what). Chain-of-thought and fine-tuning did not close the gap.
numbers: Paper reports models score lower than humans by more than 70% on average over the full set. 13 instruction-tuned models tested; human baseline 11 student volunteers (about 87 to 94% on answerability and info-access list questions as read from the figure).
limits: Conversation text only; benchmark built with LLM help plus human validation.
agent_relevance: Directly relevant who-knows-what test: track information access per character.

source: Sap, Le Bras, Fried, Choi (2022) Neural Theory-of-Mind? On the limits of social intelligence in large LMs
finding: GPT-3 did poorly on social commonsense and ToM question answering, well below humans.
numbers: Few-shot GPT-3: 55% on SocialIQa and 60% on ToMi; more than 30% below human accuracy on SocialIQa.
limits: Pre-ChatGPT model; later models do much better on standard items.
agent_relevance: Baseline for the scale-up trajectory Kosinski later reported.

source: Strachan et al. (2024) Testing theory of mind in large language models and humans (Nature Human Behaviour)
finding: On a full battery GPT-4 matched or exceeded humans on indirect requests, false belief and misdirection but struggled with faux pas. LLaMA2's faux-pas lead was illusory (bias to say 'did not know'); GPT's failure was hyperconservatism, not failed inference.
numbers: 1,907 human participants vs GPT and LLaMA2 families, repeated runs. GPT-4 endorsed 'didn't know' more for faux pas than neutral, chi2(2)=109.
limits: Text tasks only; online human sample.
agent_relevance: Moderator: willingness to commit (response bias) can explain LLM errors; probe it separately.

source: Pang et al. (2025) commentary on animal-cognition methods for LLM evaluation (via search summary)
finding: Search summary: urges comparative-psychology methods for LLM ToM tests and notes sudden jumps in newer models may reflect training for ToM tasks. Page content could not be read (only a header returned).
numbers: not read this session
limits: Secondhand.
agent_relevance: Pointer only.

source: Synthesis across Sap 2022, Kosinski 2024, Ullman 2023, Shapira 2023, Kim 2023, Strachan 2024
finding: The LLM ToM record mirrors the animal one: standard tasks pass, discriminating or perturbed tasks expose cue-based solutions. No study found this session ran corvid caching or false-belief looking paradigms on an LLM.
numbers: Sap: 55% and 60%. Kosinski: 20% to 75% of 40 tasks. Strachan: GPT-4 at or above human on 3 of 4 task types, faux pas the exception.
limits: Cross-study comparison; different tasks and models.
agent_relevance: Gap: no corvid-paradigm LLM test exists in what I found; our own eval could fill it.

source: Buttelmann et al. (2017) ignorance control as discriminating experiment
finding: Rival theory test: a simple ignorance rule predicts chance choice, a false-belief account predicts above-chance helping. Apes matched the belief account.
numbers: Ignorance condition 49.9% vs 50.1% (T+=29.00, p=.877, r=.04); false-belief 72.0% (p=.006).
limits: Behavioural-rule accounts beyond ignorance (e.g. goal inference from tugging) are not fully excluded.
agent_relevance: Design evals with a rival-rule control, as here.

source: Bugnyar et al. (2016) and Bugnyar (2011) taken together: moderators in raven work
finding: Raven effects depend on the test: strong for 'might be seen' (peephole) and 'who watched' (informed vs uninformed), absent for using barrier geometry or choosing first in some conditions.
numbers: Peephole geometry p=0.297 (n=9); stay-treatment sign test 3/5, p=1; informed matching 7/7, p=0.016.
limits: Both from one lab with 7-10 birds; none replicated independently as far as found.
agent_relevance: Effects are narrow and task-specific; expect an agent to need explicit cues, not a general ToM module.
